Dialogue 05: Retirement Income: RMD and Withdrawal Strategy
Original fictional setting: A client approaching RMD age wants to know how much to withdraw.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: The custodian sent an RMD estimate. Should I take only that amount?
Advisor: The RMD is a minimum required amount for certain accounts, not necessarily your ideal spending strategy.
Financial planner: We should coordinate the RMD with your cash-flow need, taxable income, charitable goals, and other accounts. For tax specifics, we should confirm with your CPA.
Client: Can I take it from any account?
Financial planner: That depends on the account type and IRS rules. We can help organize the question and coordinate with the custodian and tax advisor before you act.
Client: I have the custodian's notice and statements for the relevant accounts.
Financial planner: Bring those to the review. We will coordinate account-specific questions with the custodian and qualified tax adviser.
Vocabulary in this exchange: RMD: Required minimum distribution from certain retirement accounts under IRS rules, depending on age, account, and facts.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 06: Rollover Conversation: Four Options, Not One Shortcut
Original fictional setting: A client changed jobs and asks whether to roll a 401(k) into an IRA.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: Should I roll the old 401(k) into an IRA with you?
Advisor: We should compare the options before deciding.
Financial planner: The common options are leaving assets in the old plan, rolling to the new employer plan if allowed, rolling to an IRA, or cashing out. We need to compare fees, investment choices, services, creditor protections, tax impact, and your need for advice.
Client: Which one do you recommend?
Financial planner: I can make a recommendation after we document the facts and alternatives. Because an IRA rollover may increase advisory fees, we need to be especially clear about the rationale.
Client: Please include the old plan's actual fees and available services in the comparison.
Financial planner: Yes. We need the current plan information and your circumstances before documenting a recommendation and its rationale.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Recommend: Suggest a specific action or strategy based on client facts and standards. / Document: Record facts, rationale, alternatives, risks, client instructions, and follow-up.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 06: Rollover Conversation: Four Options, Not One Shortcut
Original fictional setting: A client changed jobs and asks whether to roll a 401(k) into an IRA.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: Should I roll the old 401(k) into an IRA with you?
Advisor: We should compare the options before deciding.
Financial planner: The common options are leaving assets in the old plan, rolling to the new employer plan if allowed, rolling to an IRA, or cashing out. We need to compare fees, investment choices, services, creditor protections, tax impact, and your need for advice.
Client: Which one do you recommend?
Financial planner: I can make a recommendation after we document the facts and alternatives. Because an IRA rollover may increase advisory fees, we need to be especially clear about the rationale.
Client: Please include the old plan's actual fees and available services in the comparison.
Financial planner: Yes. We need the current plan information and your circumstances before documenting a recommendation and its rationale.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Recommend: Suggest a specific action or strategy based on client facts and standards. / Document: Record facts, rationale, alternatives, risks, client instructions, and follow-up.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 07: Annuity Tradeoff: Guarantee vs Liquidity
Original fictional setting: A client asks about buying an annuity after seeing an advertisement promising lifetime income.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: This annuity says I can get guaranteed income for life. Why would I not do it?
Advisor: Income guarantees can be valuable, but the tradeoffs matter.
Financial planner: We need to review fees, surrender period, liquidity limits, inflation risk, insurer strength, tax treatment, and whether the benefit fits your income need better than other options.
Client: But the guarantee sounds safe.
Financial planner: It may reduce one type of risk, longevity risk, but it can introduce other constraints. The right question is which risk you are trying to solve and what flexibility you are willing to give up.
Client: I want to see how the surrender conditions affect access to my money.
Financial planner: We will review the actual contract, costs, guarantees, limitations, and alternatives rather than rely on the headline description.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Constraints: Limits such as income needs, legal restrictions, values preferences, concentration, liquidity, or tax concerns. / Annuity: Insurance contract that may provide income or guarantees with costs, restrictions, and conditions.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 08: Concentrated Employer Stock
Original fictional setting: A technology executive has most of their net worth in employer stock and resists diversification.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: This stock made me wealthy. I do not want to sell.
Advisor: That history matters, and so does the concentration risk going forward.
Financial planner: Your salary, bonus, unvested equity, and portfolio are all tied to the same company. Diversifying does not mean you lack confidence; it means you are protecting the wealth already created.
Client: What if I sell and it doubles?
Financial planner: That regret risk is real. We can build a staged diversification plan, use price or time triggers, and coordinate tax strategy with your CPA.
Client: Please show the effect of several approaches before I decide.
Financial planner: We will compare the risks and relevant tax questions with qualified input, without promising that any approach avoids regret or loss.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Diversification: Spreading exposure across holdings or asset classes to reduce concentration risk.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 09: Tax-Loss Harvesting: Useful but Not Magic
Original fictional setting: A client asks whether selling losses means the portfolio did not really lose money.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: If we harvest losses, does that cancel the market loss?
Advisor: No. The investment loss remains real. Tax-loss harvesting may have tax consequences or benefits depending on the facts and applicable rules; it does not cancel an economic loss.
Financial planner: We should avoid letting the tax benefit drive the investment decision by itself. We also need to watch wash-sale rules and keep the portfolio aligned with your target allocation.
Client: So it helps but does not fix everything.
Financial planner: Exactly. It is a tool, not a strategy by itself.
Client: Can we review that with my tax adviser before making a change?
Financial planner: Yes. We will coordinate the relevant facts and assess the investment and tax implications together.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Tax-loss harvesting: Selling investments at a loss to potentially offset gains, subject to tax rules and constraints.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 10: Family Pressure and Trusted Contact
Original fictional setting: An older client says a relative wants them to withdraw a large amount urgently.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: My nephew says I should send him money today for an investment.
Advisor: That sounds important. Can we slow down and understand the purpose, amount, and whether anyone is pressuring you?
Financial planner: Your choice is yours, but because this is unusual and urgent, I want to protect you from possible financial exploitation. With your permission, we can involve your trusted contact or another professional you rely on.
Client: I do not want to get anyone in trouble.
Financial planner: The goal is not to accuse anyone. The goal is to make sure the decision is truly yours and that you understand the risk before assets leave the account.
Client: I would like to discuss the request privately before doing anything.
Financial planner: We can do that and follow the firm's applicable safeguarding and escalation process, explaining the next steps and their limits.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 11: Client Complaint: 'You Never Told Me About the Fees'
Original fictional setting: A client expresses dissatisfaction after seeing advisory fees on a statement.
Professional roles: Client / Advisor / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Client: You never told me about these fees.
Advisor: I am sorry this feels surprising. I want to understand exactly what you are seeing and review what was disclosed.
Financial planner: I also need to treat your concern seriously and follow our firm's process. I will document your concern, provide the fee schedule again, and ask the supervisor to review the account history.
Client: Are you saying this is my fault?
Financial planner: No. I am saying we should review the facts carefully and make sure your concern is handled through the proper channel.
Client: Please explain when I should expect the next update on the review.
Financial planner: I will confirm the complaint process and update arrangements, and make sure the designated team acknowledges your concern.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Document: Record facts, rationale, alternatives, risks, client instructions, and follow-up. / Update: Refresh client information, risk profile, beneficiary details, or planning assumptions.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 12: Annual Review: Plan Change, Not Product Pitch
Original fictional setting: An advisor leads an annual review after the client had a new child and changed jobs.
Professional roles: Advisor / Client / Financial planner
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Advisor: Before we look at performance, let's update what changed in your life this year.
Client: We had a baby, changed jobs, and may buy a larger home.
Financial planner: Those changes affect emergency reserves, insurance needs, beneficiary designations, education planning, risk capacity, and cash-flow assumptions. The portfolio review should come after we update the plan inputs.
Client: Does that mean we need new investments?
Financial planner: Maybe, but first we update the facts. Product changes should follow the plan, not lead it.
Advisor: I will bring updated income figures and our expected housing budget.
Financial planner: Those inputs will help us assess the plan and identify questions for other qualified professionals before considering product changes.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Risk capacity: The client's financial ability to absorb loss without derailing goals. / Update: Refresh client information, risk profile, beneficiary details, or planning assumptions.
END REFERENCE

REFERENCE
Course: Financial Advice English
Professional audience: financial advisors, planners, wealth-management teams, retirement specialists, paraplanners, and client-service staff
Scope: Fictional English-language practice, not personalized financial, investment, insurance, tax, or legal advice. US terminology is used where identified; professional duties and account rules vary. Actual recommendations require current documents, client facts, applicable rules, and qualified review. No product or transaction is endorsed.
Lesson 01: Advisor English: Discovery, Scope, Trust, and Boundaries
Original fictional case: Leah tells adviser Sam, "I want to retire comfortably." She has not supplied a target date, spending estimate, or current asset and liability summary. The introductory meeting covers discovery and the proposed planning service; no engagement scope or investment recommendation has been finalized. Leah asks whether a single savings target can be supplied immediately. Sam can explain the process and request information through the approved secure channel, but cannot responsibly fill the missing facts with assumptions presented as her circumstances.
Language workshop: Turning a retirement wish into usable planning facts
Communication goal: Clarify an imprecise client goal and explain the information needed before an individualized recommendation.
Language guidance: Comfortably is a useful expression of a goal, not a defined spending amount. A date and spending estimate need a basis: today's money or future amounts, household or individual, before or after tax. Do not silently choose those meanings for the client.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): You want retirement to feel financially secure and manageable. / What timing should we use for your target retirement date? / Does that estimate cover the household or only your own spending? / Are these amounts in today's money or projected future amounts? / Which costs are essential, and which could change? / Please provide current asset, liability, and pension information through the secure channel. / An initial illustration would use assumptions that we need to verify. / We will confirm the information and service scope before a personalized recommendation. / I cannot give a reliable single target from the goal alone. / The proposed scope does not automatically include tax or legal advice. / Reviewing the information does not authorize an investment change. / The dates and spending basis affect how we interpret the target. / We can record a provisional range without treating it as confirmed spending. / Who relies on the income included in this plan? / The goal is clear; the amount, timing, and current position remain incomplete. / Does this summary distinguish your confirmed facts from our open questions?
Vocabulary: discovery meeting: An initial discussion to understand a client's circumstances and aims. / fact-find: Structured collection of information relevant to planning or advice. / planning scope: The agreed topics and services included in a planning assignment. / engagement agreement: Terms describing the professional relationship and services. / financial goal: A desired outcome expressed with relevant amount, timing, and priority. / target retirement date: The date or period the client aims to stop or reduce work. / spending estimate: An approximation of expected outgoings on a stated basis. / essential spending: Costs the client treats as necessary for basic or committed needs. / discretionary spending: Outgoings the client has greater ability to adjust. / household cash flow: Money received and paid by a household over a period. / asset summary: An account of owned resources and their relevant characteristics. / liability summary: An account of debts and other obligations. / net worth: Assets less liabilities on a defined valuation basis. / pension statement: A record of pension information issued by a plan or provider. / income source: An identified origin of household receipts. / dependant: A person relying on the client for financial support in context. / emergency reserve: Resources intended for unexpected needs, with access and amount requiring context. / time horizon: The period before or over which money is expected to be needed. / constraint: A condition limiting available choices. / priority: Relative importance assigned to a goal or need. / planning assumption: A provisional input used to explore possible outcomes. / information gap: Missing data relevant to the assessment. / secure channel: An approved protected route for exchanging sensitive information. / scope limitation: A boundary on what the engagement or analysis covers.
Speaking task: Read Leah and Sam's corrected discovery exchange. Keep the retirement date, spending basis and current financial summary as missing facts, not invented estimates. Switch roles. Stress the requests for household scope and today's-money amounts, and the separate need to agree the planning service. Read the corrected transfer twice. Preserve all three missing qualifiers: currency, household coverage and before- or after-tax basis.
Partner: Leah: Prospective client / Sam: Financial adviser
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A client says they need "forty thousand a year" but has not identified the currency, household scope, or whether the amount is before or after tax. No target has been approved.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Leah: I sometimes help a family member with bills. The amount varies. How should we include that without pretending it is a fixed monthly expense?
Sam: Include that commitment with its uncertainty and importance to you. We should understand your priorities rather than assume every optional-looking payment is something you would comfortably stop.
Leah: I will bring the records and work out what I spend now. Please leave the investments as they are while we clarify the plan.
Sam: Correct. We will review the information and proposed engagement agreement before finalizing the scope and an individualized recommendation. Today's goal is a clear starting point, not an unsupported answer.
END REFERENCE

1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Paste into a new chat, then follow the exercise one step at a time. English Ladder does not send anything to an AI service. Your chosen service's terms and any usage charges apply.

AI responses can contain mistakes. Compare feedback with the lesson and check specialist claims against the course references. Use these exercises for language practice; follow qualified guidance for actual professional decisions.

For teachers and study partners

Ask learners to respond before revealing the model. Give feedback on one meaning issue and one language pattern, then let them repeat. For mixed levels, offer the frames first and remove them in the second round.

Use the learner book for extended dialogue practice, vocabulary and collocations, reusable phrases, and explained answer keys.
